query: For high-entropy alloys intended for high-temperature applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their ability to develop and retain a protective oxide layer that provides oxidation resistance? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison that would reveal it, the observations expected relative to a baseline, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The high-temperature oxidation resistance in these HEAs is governed by the selective oxidation of key alloying elements (such as Al and Ti) that, under the influence of the multiphase microstructure (including bcc and minor σ-phase domains), enabled efficient grain boundary diffusion and the formation of a coherent, protective spinel oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A powder-metallurgy produced, multiphase high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) with bcc phases and minor σ-phase present.
generation.intervention: Exposing the alloy to elevated temperatures in an oxidizing environment (e.g., >800 °C) versus a control treatment at lower temperatures where selective oxidation is minimal.
generation.conditions: Testing under controlled atmospheric conditions with precise temperature control, comparing alloys with and without modifications that reduce the concentration of spinel-forming elements.
generation.structural_mediator: The microstructural arrangement (including the dual bcc phases and minor σ-phase) which promotes localized diffusion paths along grain boundaries for the preferential oxidation of Al and Ti to form a spinel oxide.
generation.mechanism: At temperatures above a critical threshold (~800 °C), the multiphase microstructure enhances diffusion of oxygen and facilitates the selective oxidation of elements such as Al and Ti. This results in the in-situ formation of a coherent spinel oxide layer that adheres to the substrate, thereby protecting the underlying HEA from further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloy samples exposed to high temperatures (>800 °C) will develop a distinct, spinel-structured oxide layer observable by XRD and microscopy, and demonstrate improved oxidation and wear resistance relative to baseline samples (exposed at lower temperatures or with reduced concentrations of the critical alloying elements).
generation.baseline: The same HEA processed and exposed at lower temperatures (or an alloy variant with reduced spinel-forming element concentrations), which would not form a coherent protective oxide layer and thus show higher oxidation rates and lower wear resistance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is applicable under oxidizing atmospheric conditions and at temperatures sufficiently high to activate rapid diffusion (typically above ~800 °C). It may not apply in inert atmospheres or below the critical temperature threshold.
generation.uncertainty: The precise contribution of the minor σ-phase and the detailed grain boundary chemistry to the kinetics of oxide layer formation remain to be fully quantified. Further, the influence of processing history on oxide scale adherence may also introduce variability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with the standard composition and one with a modified composition having reduced levels of Al and Ti that are critical for spinel formation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature oxidation treatments (e.g., 800–900 °C) in an oxidizing atmosphere. Measure the oxide layer formation via XRD analysis, microscopy (for layer morphology), and oxidation kinetics (e.g., weight gain measurements) over time.
measurements: XRD for phase identification of the oxide scale
Microscopy (SEM/TEM) to observe layer morphology and continuity
Weight gain measurements to assess oxidation rates
Wear resistance tests to correlate protective oxide formation with functional performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the standard HEA does not form a coherent spinel oxide layer significantly different from that on the modified alloy (or if both alloys show similar oxidation behavior and wear resistance), then the hypothesis that the selective oxidation of Al/Ti via the multiphase microstructure is governing protective oxide layer formation would be falsified.

Question: How does the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy change under reciprocating wear conditions at elevated temperatures, and what are the underlying mechanisms?. System: AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Inert gas atomisation using argon followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1050 °C for 10 min under 50 MPa compaction pressure, with passive cooling at 150 K/min until 300 °C. Test conditions: Reciprocating wear test using an SRV-Tribometer with a force of 26 N, frequency of 40 Hz, amplitude of 0.5 mm, and Al2O3 counter body (10 mm diameter) at temperatures of 22 °C, 500 °C, 650 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C for 900 s.
